title: A Public LBO
hook: Cracked windows do not get repaired faster because a nonprofit owns more side projects.
counterintuition: Public ownership can dull owner pressure, but it does not have to. The test is whether capital, staff, and meetings stop subsidizing sprawl and start strengthening the core economics.
tryThisNow: Pick one active side bet. Write the core economic measure it must improve, then name the first resource you would stop feeding if it fails that measure.
keyTakeaway: Owner-like discipline means forcing every side bet, unit, and meeting to justify the capital and attention it takes from the core, then making the core scorecard tougher.

breakdown.fastRead:
Michael finds a cracked window work order under a city grant folder. The housing nonprofit has a repair backlog, three popular pilots, and grant staff spending more time on rooftop-garden updates than on broken units. The board likes breadth. Tenants need repairs.

Bill Stiritz makes public ownership feel less like a permission slip for softness and more like a place to impose owner standards.

The public LBO idea is not about sounding harsh. It is about making public-company sprawl answer the same question an owner would ask: what capital or attention does this consume, and does it strengthen the core?
breakdown.deepRead:
Catarina walks from sealed pet-snack cartons to a sauce bottling line with a repair tag hanging from the motor. The board likes the food company's category breadth. The pet-snack sideline looks like growth. The sauce plant earns the money, needs automation, and waits because cash is trapped in a side business.

The owner scorecard changes the conversation. A broad portfolio can sound safe while it hides weak uses of capital. A side project can be charming while it borrows attention from the line that pays the bills. Public shareholders, city funders, and broad boards all create room for soft excuses unless someone forces each activity to justify what it consumes.

Pressure is not the same as discipline.

Stiritz and Ralston Purina give the idea its business weight. Ralston Purina had accumulated unrelated operations, and the supported lesson is focus tightening backed by operating rigor and deal discipline. Selling or pruning only matters if the remaining enterprise becomes economically sharper. Otherwise the company has changed shape without changing standards.

That is the limit. A loud weekly review, a divestiture announcement, or a smaller org chart can all be theater. The real test arrives after pruning: does the core get stronger, do operating measures tighten, and does capital stop leaking into protected sprawl?
breakdown.fullRead:
Sam stares at an integration dashboard with six red warning triangles. The public software company bought small tools for years because each acquisition gave the market a story. None of them integrates cleanly. Enterprise renewals are slipping because the flagship platform is less reliable than customers were promised.

In the postmortem, he asks which acquired tool changes renewal economics. Two vanity acquisitions fail the test. Engineers move back to core platform reliability. The action looks less exciting than another purchase, but it finally makes capital and attention answer to the same owner-like measure.

Ralston Purina gives the public LBO idea its bite because sprawl had to stop receiving automatic subsidy. Bill Stiritz used operating rigor and deal discipline to create private-equity-like economics inside a public company. The phrase matters only if you keep the operating half. Public-market discipline is not a costume; it is a tougher scorecard applied where public-company comfort often lets unrelated businesses linger.

Ask what the side bet consumes before asking whether it sounds promising.

Anke sees it in a regional fitness chain. The boutique class brands make the menu look broader, but utilization audits show trainers stretched thin and maintenance logs piling up in the core gyms. After three audits, she closes two low-return brands and installs a weekly dashboard for the core model. The pruning is only half the move. The tougher operating dashboard is what proves the standard changed.

Pablo sees another version at an airport services contractor. You expect the lounge-service invoice to be the growth engine because it is new and visible. Then the working-capital schedule shows margin leakage, while the baggage-handling renewal has better owner economics. Cutting the lounge add-on protects the renewal that actually funds the division.

This is the danger with sprawl: it usually has defenders. A pilot has a champion. A sideline has a press release. An acquisition has a team. An unrelated unit has someone who remembers why it once made sense. Owner-like discipline does not sneer at those arguments. It asks them to bring a measure.

The public setting makes that measure more important, not less. When many owners are distant and every sideline can claim a story, leaders have to make the economic test visible enough for weak projects to lose honestly.

The measure has to connect to the core. Repair backlog. Automation payback. Renewal economics. Trainer utilization. Working capital. Supplier savings. If the side bet cannot improve one of those, it should stop receiving staff time, capital, or executive attention.

Public does not have to mean soft. Public means the scorecard must be visible enough that softness has fewer places to hide.

examples.title: Michael Closes the Rooftop Garden Pilot

planSpec.domain: publicly funded housing nonprofit with unrelated pilot programs
planSpec.audience: an executive director accountable to a broad board and city funders
planSpec.stakes: core repair backlog growing while pilots absorb grant staff
planSpec.requiredBeat: Michael pins each pilot to a repair-backlog dollar and closes the popular rooftop-garden expansion because it does not strengthen the core housing economics.

examples.scenario: A cracked window work order sits under a city grant folder while Michael reviews the pilot list before the board meeting. Grant staff hours are flowing to a rooftop-garden expansion, and the repair backlog keeps growing. City funders like the pilot's photographs. Tenants keep calling about broken units. Michael must decide whether to preserve the popular expansion or pin each pilot to a repair-backlog dollar and close the one that does not strengthen core housing economics.
examples.whatToDo: Tie each pilot to a repair-backlog dollar, then close the rooftop-garden expansion if it does not improve core housing economics. Move grant staff back to repairs that tenants can feel.
examples.whyItMatters: The nonprofit's core is usable housing. A popular pilot that absorbs staff while repairs pile up is sprawl, even when it photographs well for funders.

examples.title: Catarina Funds the Sauce Line

planSpec.domain: listed specialty food company deciding whether to sell a pet-snack sideline
planSpec.audience: a CFO whose board likes the appearance of category breadth
planSpec.stakes: cash trapped in the sideline could fund automation in the profitable sauce plant
planSpec.requiredBeat: Catarina walks from the pet-snack inventory racks to the sauce bottling line and marks which asset earns automation capital under the owner scorecard.

examples.scenario: Sealed pet-snack cartons are stacked beside a sauce-line repair tag when Catarina starts the plant walk. The board category memo praises breadth, but the sideline traps cash while the profitable sauce plant waits for an automation quote. She must decide whether the category story stays intact or which asset earns automation capital under an owner scorecard: inventory racks that impress the board or the bottling line that funds the company.
examples.whatToDo: Walk the sideline inventory and the sauce line together, then fund the asset with stronger owner economics. Sell or stop feeding the sideline if it blocks automation in the core plant.
examples.whyItMatters: Breadth can hide weak capital use. The sauce line earns the next dollar because it improves the business that actually produces returns.

examples.title: Sam Sunsets the Vanity Acquisitions

planSpec.domain: software company after years of buying small tools that never integrate
planSpec.audience: a public-company product chief with six underused acquisitions
planSpec.stakes: engineering attention split while the flagship product misses enterprise renewals
planSpec.requiredBeat: Sam asks which acquired tool changes renewal economics, sunsets two vanity acquisitions, and moves engineers back to the core platform reliability work.

examples.scenario: "Which tool changes renewal economics?" Sam asks after the postmortem opens on an integration dashboard with six red warning triangles. The software company bought small tools for years, and every team can defend its own acquisition. The renewal report says enterprise customers are leaving because the flagship platform is unreliable. Sam sunsets two vanity acquisitions and moves engineers back to core reliability work.
examples.whatToDo: Test every acquired tool against renewal economics. Sunset the tools that fail and move engineers to the reliability work that protects the flagship platform.
examples.whyItMatters: Acquisitions consume engineering attention long after the announcement. If they do not improve renewals, they are pulling resources away from the product customers pay to keep.

examples.title: Anke Closes Two Boutique Class Brands

planSpec.domain: regional fitness chain pruning boutique class brands after expansion
planSpec.audience: an operations VP facing franchisees who like the wider menu
planSpec.stakes: trainer utilization and equipment maintenance are weakening the core gym model
planSpec.requiredBeat: After three utilization audits, Anke closes two low-return class brands and installs a stricter weekly operating dashboard for the core gyms.

examples.scenario: Unused reformer machines line the studio mirror while Anke reviews the third utilization audit. Franchisees like the wider class menu, but trainer hours are scattered and the maintenance log for the core gyms is getting worse. Before the next franchise call, she compares utilization, equipment costs, and member visits. After three audits, Anke closes two low-return class brands and installs a stricter weekly dashboard for the core gyms.
examples.whatToDo: Close the class brands that fail utilization and maintenance tests, then install a weekly dashboard for the core gym model. Make the pruning show up in operating measures.
examples.whyItMatters: Focus only matters if standards get tougher afterward. Closing weak brands frees trainers and maintenance attention for the model that carries the chain.

examples.title: Pablo Cuts the Lounge Add-On

planSpec.domain: airport services contractor reviewing lounge, cleaning, and baggage add-ons
planSpec.audience: a division manager whose public parent company rewards revenue breadth
planSpec.stakes: margin leakage in side contracts threatens the core baggage-handling renewal
planSpec.requiredBeat: You expect the newest lounge contract to be the growth engine; Pablo reveals the working-capital schedule and cuts it because the core baggage renewal has better owner economics.

examples.scenario: You expect the lounge-service invoice below the baggage tug to be the growth engine. Pablo thought so too, until the working-capital schedule showed cash trapped in side contracts while the core baggage-handling renewal carried better owner economics. The parent company rewards revenue breadth, but the renewal is due in two weeks. Pablo must decide whether to keep funding the new lounge add-on or cut it before it weakens the contract that funds the division.
examples.whatToDo: Put the working-capital schedule beside the baggage renewal, then cut the lounge add-on if it leaks margin. Protect the contract with the better owner economics.
examples.whyItMatters: Revenue breadth can hide cash strain. The baggage renewal deserves capital and attention because it funds the division, while the side contract drains working capital.

examples.title: Hannah Centralizes Terms, Not Medicine

planSpec.domain: regional veterinary group centralizing procurement after scattered clinic acquisitions
planSpec.audience: a CEO who wants scale benefits without smothering clinic medicine
planSpec.stakes: drug costs and local autonomy both at risk after acquisitions
planSpec.requiredBeat: What would an owner keep strict and what would she leave local? Hannah centralizes supplier terms and kills weak side ventures while leaving medical protocols with clinic leads.

examples.scenario: What would an owner keep strict and what would she leave local? Hannah asks that with a vaccine refrigerator temperature strip beside a supplier rebate sheet. The veterinary group has acquired scattered clinics, drug costs are rising, and clinic leads fear losing medical judgment. Hannah has to choose between centralizing everything and a narrower owner scorecard: centralize supplier terms, kill weak side ventures, and leave medical protocols with clinic leads.
examples.whatToDo: Centralize supplier terms and rebate tracking, kill side ventures that do not improve clinic economics, and leave medical protocols with clinic leads under clear quality standards.
examples.whyItMatters: Owner-like discipline should capture scale benefits without smothering local medicine. Procurement belongs at the center; clinical judgment stays where patient facts live.

questions.prompt: A public company keeps unrelated side businesses because they make the portfolio look broad, while the core plant waits for automation capital. What is the best diagnosis?
choices: Sprawl is receiving capital that should be tested against the core economics.
The company should keep every side business because public investors like breadth.
Automation should wait until all side businesses agree to fund it.
questions.explanation: The side businesses need to justify the capital they trap. Breadth is not enough if the core plant offers stronger owner economics.

questions.prompt: A housing nonprofit has a growing repair backlog and a popular rooftop-garden pilot using grant staff. What should the director do?
choices: Keep the pilot because funders like visible innovation.
Tie the pilot to repair-backlog dollars and close it if it does not strengthen housing economics.
Pause all repairs until the board finishes reviewing every program.
questions.explanation: The repair backlog is the core measure. A popular pilot deserves staff only if it strengthens that core, not because it photographs well.

questions.prompt: A software company owns six acquired tools, but enterprise renewals are slipping because the flagship platform is unreliable. Which move fits?
choices: Keep every tool because acquisitions show growth.
Assign one engineer to each tool so no team feels abandoned.
Sunset tools that do not improve renewal economics and move engineers to platform reliability.
questions.explanation: Renewal economics define the core. Tools that do not support renewals consume engineering attention needed by the product customers are leaving over.

questions.prompt: A fitness chain closes two weak class brands after a utilization audit but keeps the same loose gym maintenance routine and vague trainer metrics. What is missing?
choices: Operating rigor after pruning.
A broader menu to replace the closed brands.
A softer message for franchisees.
questions.explanation: Pruning is only half the move. If the core gym dashboard does not get tougher, the company changed shape without improving discipline.

questions.prompt: An airport services division has a new lounge add-on that boosts revenue but leaks working capital before payroll week. The baggage renewal is due soon and has better owner economics. What should happen?
choices: Keep the lounge add-on because new revenue is always useful.
Cut the lounge add-on and protect the baggage renewal.
Add another side contract to offset the cash strain.
questions.explanation: Revenue breadth is weaker than owner economics. The baggage renewal deserves attention because it funds the division without the side-contract cash leak.

questions.prompt: A CEO sells two unrelated units, announces a cleaner portfolio, and then lets weak core metrics drift for two quarters. Why is the improvement incomplete?
choices: The sale should have included every unit outside the headquarters city.
The company needed a more dramatic announcement to signal discipline.
Portfolio action did not lead to a tougher operating scorecard.
questions.explanation: Selling units can clarify focus, but operating rigor proves the standard changed. Without tougher core metrics, pruning becomes a shape change.

questions.prompt: A public parent company rewards division heads for revenue breadth during quarterly reviews. One division's side contracts lower margin and distract managers from a renewal that funds the unit. What pressure is at work?
choices: Public-company softness is allowing breadth to hide weak capital use.
The division head is too focused on renewal economics.
The side contracts must be retained because public companies need visible growth.
questions.explanation: The incentive rewards breadth even when economics weaken. Owner-like discipline would force side contracts to justify cash and attention against the renewal.

questions.prompt: A veterinary group centralizes every clinic decision after acquisitions, including medical protocols, to prove discipline. What mistake does that show?
choices: Scale benefits are never worth pursuing in professional services.
The center is confusing owner discipline with control of decisions best left local.
Supplier terms should be negotiated separately by each clinic.
questions.explanation: Owner discipline should centralize supplier economics and weak side ventures, not smother medical judgment. The center has to know which controls actually improve economics.

questions.prompt: Two restructuring plans are offered. Plan A sells side units but leaves core metrics vague. Plan B sells weak side units and installs weekly operating measures for the core. Which is better?
choices: Plan A, because selling assets is the main evidence of discipline.
Plan B, because focus only counts when the core scorecard becomes tougher afterward.
Neither, because a public company should avoid owner-like pressure.
questions.explanation: Plan B connects pruning to operating rigor. Plan A may look decisive, but it does not prove capital and attention will work harder inside the remaining business.

reviewCards.front: A public company keeps side businesses for breadth while the core needs capital. What do you ask?
reviewCards.back: Ask what each side business consumes and which core economic measure it improves. If it cannot answer, it should stop receiving capital or attention.

reviewCards.front: A company sells two weak side units, then leaves the core with loose metrics. Why is pruning alone not enough?
reviewCards.back: Pruning has to be followed by operating rigor. The remaining core should get clearer metrics, tighter resource use, and a harder standard after the side bets are gone.

reviewCards.front: What is public-company softness in practical terms?
reviewCards.back: It is the tolerance that lets weak units, side projects, or broad portfolios keep consuming resources because no owner-like test forces them to justify the cost.

reviewCards.front: How do you avoid turning owner discipline into harsh style?
reviewCards.back: Tie every cut to a measure: backlog, payback, renewal economics, utilization, working capital, or supplier savings. The measure keeps discipline from becoming theater.

reviewCards.front: A side bet has a champion and a good story. What would an owner-like scorecard require?
reviewCards.back: It would require proof that the side bet improves the core economics enough to justify its capital, staff time, and executive attention. Story is not enough.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: Learn to force sprawl through an owner-like scorecard. The skill is tying every side bet to a core economic measure and then making the operating standard tougher after pruning.

ifThenPlans.plan: If a side unit is defended by breadth, then ask which core economic measure it improves and what capital it traps.
If you prune a project, then install one weekly metric that proves the core became stronger afterward.
If a pilot absorbs staff while core work backs up, then translate the pilot into backlog dollars before renewing it.
If an acquired tool splits engineering attention, then test it against renewal economics before assigning another sprint to it.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Pick one active side bet and write the core economic measure it must improve. If it cannot improve that measure, write the first resource you would stop feeding it.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, review one project, unit, or meeting that exists outside the core. Name its resource cost, its core measure, and the operating metric that should improve if it stays.

memorableLines.text: Pressure is not the same as discipline.
memorableLines.why: The line separates owner standards from harsh style in a compressed way.

memorableLines.text: Ask what the side bet consumes before asking whether it sounds promising.
memorableLines.why: It gives readers a practical first question for sprawl.

memorableLines.text: Public does not have to mean soft.
memorableLines.why: It lands the public-company tension in six plain words.
